title: Projective Extensions and the Little Group Method

items.title: "Projective representations and normalized factor sets"
items.statement: For a finite group Q and a nonzero finite-dimensional complex space V, a normalized projective representation is a map P:Q→GL(V) with P(1)=1 and P(q)P(r)=α(q,r)P(qr) for scalars α(q,r)∈C×. The function α is its factor set; in this convention the scalar multiplies P(qr).

references.title: Britta Späth, Reduction theorems for some global-local conjectures, §1.A–B, pp. 2–6
Tammo tom Dieck, Representation Theory, §§4.2–4.3 and 4.6, pp. 55–59, 64–65

items.title: "The factor set satisfies the two-cocycle equation"
items.statement: The factor set of a normalized projective representation satisfies α(1,q)=α(q,1)=1 and α(q,r)α(qr,s)=α(r,s)α(q,rs).

references.title: Britta Späth, Reduction theorems for some global-local conjectures, §1.A–B, pp. 2–6

items.strategy: Compare (P(q)P(r))P(s) with P(q)(P(r)P(s)); cancel the invertible P(qrs). The identity equations follow from P(1)=1. Read the resulting multiplicative equation as the normalized cocycle condition for the trivial Q-action on C×; the published additive convention is the same equation written multiplicatively.

items.title: "Rephasing changes factor sets by coboundaries"
items.statement: For c:Q→C× with c(1)=1, P_c(q)=c(q)P(q) has factor set α_c(q,r)=c(q)c(r)c(qr)^{-1}α(q,r). Hence rephasing preserves the cohomology class.

references.title: Britta Späth, Reduction theorems for some global-local conjectures, §1.A–B, pp. 2–6

items.strategy: Substitute P_c in the defining product and cancel P_c(qr). The displayed scalar is the multiplicative coboundary δc times α. Conversely any prescribed cohomologous factor set is reached by such a normalized cochain.

items.title: "Twisted group algebra of a factor set"
items.statement: For a finite group Q and normalized C×-valued two-cocycle α, C^α[Q] is the complex vector space with basis u_q (q∈Q), proposed product u_q u_r=α(q,r)u_{qr}, and unit u_1. The following lemma verifies associativity and the module interpretation.

references.title: Britta Späth, Reduction theorems for some global-local conjectures, §1.A–B, pp. 2–6

items.title: "Projective representations and twisted algebra modules"
items.statement: C^α[Q] is an associative unital algebra. Nonzero finite-dimensional left C^α[Q]-modules are precisely normalized projective Q-representations with factor set α; the zero module is the common zero object, and this algebra is semisimple over C.

references.title: Britta Späth, Reduction theorems for some global-local conjectures, §1.A–B, pp. 2–6

items.strategy: Compute (u_q u_r)u_s and u_q(u_r u_s); the cocycle equation makes them equal, and normalization makes u_1 a unit. Each u_q is invertible, with inverse a scalar multiple of u_{q^{-1}}. A module sends u_q to P(q), and the multiplication law gives exactly the projective relation; the construction reverses. For semisimplicity, given a submodule and any linear projection onto it, average its conjugates by the invertible operators P(q); scalar factors cancel in conjugation, giving a module-equivariant splitting. The zero module is permitted for every fixed multiplier α but has no uniquely recoverable multiplier, which is why the representation correspondence is stated for nonzero modules.

items.title: "An invariant irreducible normal representation yields projective inertia operators"
items.statement: Let N◁G be finite groups, let ρ:N→GL(S) be irreducible, and I=I_G(ρ). There are operators P(i) on S with P(n)=ρ(n), P(ni)=ρ(n)P(i), P(in)=P(i)ρ(n), and P(i)P(j)=α(iN,jN)P(ij), where α is a normalized two-cocycle on I/N. The projective operators live on I; their factor set descends to I/N. Two normalized choices differ by a scalar cochain on I/N.

references.title: Britta Späth, Reduction theorems for some global-local conjectures, §1.A–B, pp. 2–6
Tammo tom Dieck, Representation Theory, §§4.2–4.3 and 4.6, pp. 55–59, 64–65

items.strategy: Use the published left-conjugation convention ρ^i(n)=ρ(i^{-1}ni). Choose a normalized transversal t of I/N and an intertwiner T_t satisfying T_tρ(n)T_t^{-1}=ρ(tnt^{-1}), with T_1=1. Define P(nt)=ρ(n)T_t. Show this is independent of the expression and has both N-equivariance identities. P(i)P(j) and P(ij) intertwine the same irreducible N-module, so their ratio is scalar by Schur. The N-equivariance identities show this scalar is unchanged if i or j is multiplied by N, hence descends to Q=I/N. Associativity and normalization give the cocycle equation. For another normalized family P′, Schur makes P′(i)P(i)^{-1} scalar and the N-identities make this scalar constant on N-cosets.

items.title: "The Clifford obstruction class of an invariant irreducible representation"
items.statement: For finite groups N◁G and ρ∈Irr(N) with inertia group I, the Clifford obstruction to extending ρ to I is the class [α]∈H²(I/N,C×), with trivial quotient action, of the factor set of normalized projective inertia operators. It is independent of the operator choices and of replacing ρ by an equivalent module.

references.title: Britta Späth, Reduction theorems for some global-local conjectures, §1.A–B, pp. 2–6

items.title: "An invariant irreducible representation extends to its inertia group exactly when the Clifford obstruction vanishes"
items.statement: For finite groups N◁G, an irreducible N-representation ρ extends to a genuine representation of its inertia group I if and only if its Clifford obstruction [α] in H²(I/N,C×) is zero. In particular this holds when I=N.

references.title: Britta Späth, Reduction theorems for some global-local conjectures, §1.A–B, pp. 2–6
Tammo tom Dieck, Representation Theory, §§4.2–4.3 and 4.6, pp. 55–59, 64–65

items.strategy: A genuine extension is a valid normalized operator family with α=1. Conversely, if [α]=0, choose normalized c:Q→C× with δc=α^{-1}; rephase P(i) by c(iN). The new factor set is 1, and c(1)=1 preserves the restriction to N. For I=N the quotient and its cocycle are trivial and the original ρ is the extension.

items.title: "The twisted product of a normalized cocycle is a central extension"
items.statement: For a normalized cocycle α on Q, E_α=Q×C× with (q,z)(r,w)=(qr,α(q,r)zw) is a group. Its kernel C× is central and E_α/C×≅Q; E_α need not be finite.

references.title: Britta Späth, Reduction theorems for some global-local conjectures, §1.A–B, pp. 2–6

items.strategy: Compute both threefold products; equality is exactly the cocycle identity. The unit is (1,1). The inverse of (q,z) is (q^{-1},α(q,q^{-1})^{-1}z^{-1}); the cocycle equation at (q,q^{-1},q) gives α(q,q^{-1})=α(q^{-1},q), so it is also a left inverse. The projection to Q is a surjective homomorphism with central kernel {(1,z)}.

items.title: "The cocycle central extension linearizes a projective representation"
items.statement: Projective Q-representations P with factor set α correspond to ordinary E_α-representations D for which D(1,z)=z·1, by D(q,z)=zP(q) and P(q)=D(q,1).

references.title: Britta Späth, Reduction theorems for some global-local conjectures, §1.A–B, pp. 2–6

items.strategy: Using the product in E_α, calculate D(q,z)D(r,w)=zwα(q,r)P(qr)=D((q,z)(r,w)). Conversely the prescribed central action and (q,1)(r,1)=(qr,α(q,r)) force P(q)P(r)=α(q,r)P(qr). These constructions are inverse on maps and intertwiners.

items.title: "The projective Clifford correspondence for an invariant irreducible representation"
items.statement: Let N◁G be finite groups, ρ∈Irr(N) on S, I=I_G(ρ), and fix projective inertia operators P with quotient factor set α. Irreducible representations of I whose restriction contains ρ correspond bijectively to irreducible projective representations of I/N with factor set α^{-1}, by U≅S⊗M with the linear I-action P(i)⊗M(iN). Induction from I then bijects these with Irr(G|ρ), modulo the ordinary Clifford conjugacy choice. If I=N, the quotient contributes its unique trivial module; if α is trivialized, this reduces to Gallagher’s ordinary extension description.

references.title: Britta Späth, Reduction theorems for some global-local conjectures, §1.A–B, pp. 2–6
Tammo tom Dieck, Representation Theory, §§4.2–4.3 and 4.6, pp. 55–59, 64–65

items.strategy: For U over ρ, Clifford makes U|N ρ-isotypical; put M=Hom_N(S,U) and use published evaluation E:S⊗M→U. Define M(i)f=U(i)fP(i)^{-1}. Check N-equivariance, M(n)=1, and M(ij)=α(iN,jN)M(i)M(j), so M factors through I/N with inverse multiplier. Evaluation is I-linear for P⊗M. Conversely an α^{-1}-projective M gives a genuine tensor I-module restricting to copies of ρ. The published subspace correspondence says I-stable submodules correspond exactly to projective-stable multiplicity subspaces, proving irreducibility both ways and inverse constructions. Apply the published Clifford induction and recovery lemmas. Treat I=N, α=1, and I=G explicitly.

items.title: "The little group method for a semidirect product with abelian kernel"
items.statement: Let G=A⋊H be a finite group with A abelian. For θ∈Â let H_θ={h∈H:θ(h^{-1}ah)=θ(a) for all a∈A} and I_θ=A⋊H_θ. The formula θ̃(ah)=θ(a) is a linear extension to I_θ. Up to isomorphism, the irreducible G-representations are exactly Ind_{I_θ}^G(θ̃⊗Infl_{H_θ}^{I_θ}σ), for one θ from each H-orbit in Â and σ∈Irr(H_θ); degrees are [H:H_θ]dimσ. In this split case the obstruction class vanishes, while the preceding projective correspondence gives the correction for a nonsplit invariant type.

references.title: Tammo tom Dieck, Representation Theory, §§4.2–4.3 and 4.6, pp. 55–59, 64–65
Britta Späth, Reduction theorems for some global-local conjectures, §1.A–B, pp. 2–6

items.strategy: Verify θ̃((a,h)(b,k))=θ(a·hbh^{-1})=θ(a)θ(b) for h∈H_θ, so it is a homomorphism. Since A is abelian, every A-type is one-dimensional. Gallagher identifies I_θ-irreducibles above θ as θ̃⊗inflated σ. Ordinary Clifford induction gives irreducibility, exhaustion, and the H-orbit identifications; the degree formula follows from induction. Check H_θ=H, H_θ=1, and A=1. The explicit extension gives α=1, making the projective correction unnecessary in this split case.

title: Projective Extensions and the Little Group Method — Examples

items.title: "The quaternion group as a cocycle central extension of C2 x C2"
items.statement: Q8/{±1}≅C2×C2. Its faithful two-dimensional complex representation yields a projective representation of C2×C2 whose factor set is nontrivial: the lifts of the two generators anticommute. The ±1-valued subgroup of its cocycle central extension is Q8.

references.title: Britta Späth, Reduction theorems for some global-local conjectures, §1.A–B, pp. 2–6
Tammo tom Dieck, Representation Theory, §§4.2–4.3 and 4.6, pp. 55–59, 64–65

items.strategy: Write x=iZ and y=jZ, and take section s(1)=1,s(x)=i,s(y)=j,s(xy)=k. Set α(q,r)=s(q)s(r)s(qr)^{-1}∈{±1}. Compute α(x,x)=α(y,y)=−1, α(x,y)=1, α(y,x)=−1. The 2×2 matrices I↦diag(i,−i), J↦[[0,1],[-1,0]] satisfy I²=J²=−1 and IJ=−JI; their values on s(q) have this multiplier. The eight elements (q,±1) in E_α multiply as Q8. A coboundary on the abelian quotient would have symmetric commutator, so α is nontrivial.

items.title: "An invariant central character of the quaternion group with no linear extension"
items.statement: The nontrivial character θ of Z(Q8)={±1}, with θ(−1)=−1, is Q8-invariant but has no linear extension to Q8.

references.title: Britta Späth, Reduction theorems for some global-local conjectures, §1.A–B, pp. 2–6
Tammo tom Dieck, Representation Theory, §§4.2–4.3 and 4.6, pp. 55–59, 64–65

items.strategy: Centrality makes θ invariant. Any one-dimensional character of Q8 kills its commutator subgroup, which contains −1 since [i,j]=−1. Thus an extension cannot take −1 to −1. The preceding projective factor set has nonzero obstruction, in agreement with the extension criterion.

items.title: "Little groups compute the irreducible characters of a dihedral group"
items.statement: For D_{2n}=C_n⋊C2 with inversion (n≥1), the characters θ_k(r)=exp(2πik/n) lie in orbits {k,−k}. Each fixed k (2k=0 mod n) gives two linear characters; every other orbit gives one irreducible of degree two, induced from C_n. These exhaust Irr(D_{2n}), including n=1,2.

references.title: Tammo tom Dieck, Representation Theory, §§4.2–4.3 and 4.6, pp. 55–59, 64–65

items.strategy: The reflection sends θ_k to θ_{−k}. Fixed k have full stabilizer C2 and its two linear irreducibles give two extensions. Nonfixed k have trivial stabilizer in C2, so the little-group formula is Ind_{C_n}^{D_{2n}}θ_k of degree two, with k and −k equivalent. Count degrees: if f is the number of fixed k, there are 2f linear and (n−f)/2 degree-two representations; their square sum is 2f+4(n−f)/2=2n. For n=1,2 all k are fixed.

items.title: "Rephasing the trivial projective representation of C2 by a coboundary"
items.statement: For Q=C2={1,t}, the trivial one-dimensional projective representation P(t)=1 has α=1. Rephasing by c(1)=1,c(t)=i gives P_c(t)=i and α_c(t,t)=−1=δc(t,t), so the two factor sets have the same zero class.

references.title: Britta Späth, Reduction theorems for some global-local conjectures, §1.A–B, pp. 2–6

items.strategy: Compute P_c(t)^2=i²=−1 and P_c(1)=1. Since t²=1, the unique nontrivial factor-set value is −1. The coboundary formula gives c(t)c(t)c(1)^{-1}=−1. Multiplying P_c(t) by −i returns the genuine representation.

items.title: Monomial characters and M-groups
items.statement: A finite-dimensional complex G-representation or character is monomial if it is induced from a one-dimensional representation λ of some subgroup H≤G. A finite group is an M-group if every irreducible complex character is monomial. The assertion concerns actual irreducibles, not arbitrary integral virtual-character sums.

references.title: Tammo tom Dieck, Representation Theory, §§4.2–4.3 and 4.6, pp. 55–59, 64–65
Wen-Wei Li, Yanqi Lake Lectures on Algebra I, §§12.5, 14.3, pp. 146–148, 162–164
SLMath, Character Theory of Finite Groups, Ch. 9, slides 374–404

items.title: Coset-basis monomial matrices
items.statement: For finite G, if V=Ind_H^G λ for a one-dimensional λ, a basis indexed by left cosets G/H makes each group element act by a monomial matrix: exactly one nonzero entry in every row and column. Conversely, an irreducible representation with such a basis is induced from the one-dimensional action on a basis line stabilizer.

references.title: Tammo tom Dieck, Representation Theory, §§4.2–4.3 and 4.6, pp. 55–59, 64–65

items.strategy: Choose a representative of each left coset and its tensor basis vector. Left multiplication sends each representative to another times h∈H, so its matrix has one nonzero scalar λ(h) in each row and column. Conversely group elements permute basis lines; each orbit spans an invariant subspace, so irreducibility forces a single orbit. The stabilizer H of one line acts there by λ, and the coset-basis map Ind_H^G λ→V is a nonzero surjective map between spaces of the same dimension, hence an isomorphism.

items.title: Faithful irreducibles induce from proper inertia groups
items.statement: Let V be a faithful irreducible complex representation of finite G, and let A◁G be abelian but not contained in Z(G). For every constituent λ of V|A, its inertia group I_G(λ) is proper in G, and V≅Ind_{I_G(λ)}^G W for a suitable irreducible W over λ.

references.title: Tammo tom Dieck, Representation Theory, §§4.2–4.3 and 4.6, pp. 55–59, 64–65
Wen-Wei Li, Yanqi Lake Lectures on Algebra I, §§12.5, 14.3, pp. 146–148, 162–164

items.strategy: All A-constituents are linear. If the inertia group were G, Clifford would make V|A λ-isotypical, so every a∈A acts as λ(a)1. Then every [g,a] acts trivially; faithfulness forces [g,a]=1 for all g,a, contradicting A⊄Z(G). Thus I_G(λ)<G, and the published Clifford correspondence supplies W and the induction isomorphism.

items.title: A noncentral abelian normal layer in a supersolvable group
items.statement: Every finite nonabelian supersolvable group G, where the prime-order normal-series terms are normal in the whole group, contains an abelian normal subgroup A not contained in Z(G). The same holds in any nonabelian quotient of G.

references.title: Tammo tom Dieck, Representation Theory, §§4.2–4.3 and 4.6, pp. 55–59, 64–65
Wen-Wei Li, Yanqi Lake Lectures on Algebra I, §§12.5, 14.3, pp. 146–148, 162–164

items.strategy: A quotient of a supersolvable group is supersolvable by projecting and deleting repeated terms of a cyclic-factor normal series. Since G is nonabelian, G/Z(G) is nontrivial. In a supersolvable normal series of this quotient, take the first nontrivial term C; it is nontrivial cyclic and normal. Let A be its preimage in G. Then A◁G and A/Z(G)≅C is cyclic. A group with central subgroup Z(G) and cyclic quotient A/Z(G) is abelian: write all elements z a^k and commute them. Since C≠1, A⊄Z(G). Repeat after any quotient.

items.title: Induction commutes with quotient inflation
items.statement: Let K◁G, let π:G→G/K, let H≥K and write H̄=H/K. For every complex H̄-module W, Infl_{G/K}^G(Ind_{H̄}^{G/K}W)≅Ind_H^G(Infl_{H̄}^H W). In particular, inflation of a monomial irreducible remains monomial.

references.title: Tammo tom Dieck, Representation Theory, §§4.2–4.3 and 4.6, pp. 55–59, 64–65
Wen-Wei Li, Yanqi Lake Lectures on Algebra I, §§12.5, 14.3, pp. 146–148, 162–164

items.strategy: Use the published covariant-function model. An H-covariant function f:G→W is constant on right K-cosets because K≤H acts trivially on inflated W; hence it descends uniquely to f̄:G/K→W. The H-covariance law becomes exactly H/K-covariance, and the left G action descends to the quotient action. Pullback along π is the inverse map. A linear W inflates to a linear H-module, proving the monomial consequence.

items.title: Finite supersolvable groups are M-groups
items.statement: Every finite supersolvable group, with a G-normal series of prime-order factors as in the standard supersolvable convention, is an M-group: each irreducible complex representation is induced from a linear character of a subgroup.

references.title: Tammo tom Dieck, Representation Theory, §§4.2–4.3 and 4.6, pp. 55–59, 64–65
Wen-Wei Li, Yanqi Lake Lectures on Algebra I, §§12.5, 14.3, pp. 146–148, 162–164

items.strategy: Induct on |G|. For an irreducible V with kernel K≠1, the quotient G/K is supersolvable and smaller; apply induction there, then the explicit induction–inflation lemma. For faithful V, if G is abelian then V is linear. Otherwise the normal-layer lemma gives A◁G abelian and noncentral. The faithful-inertia lemma gives V=Ind_I^G W with I<G. Subgroups of a supersolvable group are supersolvable by intersecting the normal series and noting each quotient embeds in a cyclic factor. By induction W=Ind_L^I λ with λ linear. Transitivity yields V=Ind_L^G λ. The base |G|=1 and possible I=1 are included.

items.title: Brauer monomial induction for virtual characters
items.statement: Every virtual complex character of a finite group G is an integral linear combination of characters Ind_H^G λ with H a p-elementary subgroup for some prime p and λ a linear character of H. This does not assert that an individual irreducible is one of these summands or that G is an M-group.

references.title: Tammo tom Dieck, Representation Theory, §§4.2–4.3 and 4.6, pp. 55–59, 64–65
Wen-Wei Li, Yanqi Lake Lectures on Algebra I, §§12.5, 14.3, pp. 146–148, 162–164

items.strategy: For G=1, every virtual character is an integer multiple of its unique linear character, which is induced from the trivial subgroup (itself), a p-elementary group for any prime. For |G|>1, repeat the published Brauer induction-ideal argument using the sound elementary-detection and ideal lemmas. For each p dividing |G|, write |G|=p^{n_p}l_p with p∤l_p; detection gives l_p·1_G in the induction ideal from p-elementary subgroups. The integers l_p have gcd 1, so Bézout gives 1_G in the full elementary induction ideal; the ideal property then puts every virtual character there. Every p-elementary subgroup E=C×P is supersolvable by the published group lemma, and the local supersolvable M-group theorem writes each of its irreducibles as Ind_K^E λ for K≤E and λ linear. Such K is p-elementary: the coprime-order components of each element of K lie in K, giving K=(K∩C)×(K∩P), with cyclic p-prime first factor. Expand each virtual subgroup character with integer coefficients and use induction transitivity. This proves the full Brauer monomial consequence without relying on the published supersolvable theorem’s omitted induction–inflation step. Coefficients may be negative, so this does not prove that G is an M-group.

items.title: Kernel of an induced module and its inducing subgroup
items.statement: If H≤G and W is a nonzero finite-dimensional complex H-module, then ker(Ind_H^G W)=⋂_{g∈G}g(ker W)g^{-1}, in particular it lies in core_G(H)⊆H. For W=1_H, this is the kernel of the permutation action on G/H.

references.title: SLMath, Character Theory of Finite Groups, Ch. 9, slides 374–404

items.strategy: Write Ind_H^G W=⊕_{t∈G/H}t⊗W. An element acting trivially must fix each direct summand, hence every coset; this puts it in core_G(H). On the summand t⊗W it acts as t⊗W(t^{-1}xt); it is the identity exactly when t^{-1}xt∈ker W. Intersect over cosets. The reverse implication gives identity on every summand, proving equality. The case H=G is immediate.

items.title: Taketa theorem for finite M-groups
items.statement: A finite M-group is solvable. More precisely, if it has r distinct irreducible complex character degrees, its derived length is at most r.

references.title: SLMath, Character Theory of Finite Groups, Ch. 9, slides 374–404
Tammo tom Dieck, Representation Theory, §§4.2–4.3 and 4.6, pp. 55–59, 64–65

items.strategy: Order distinct degrees 1=d_1<⋯<d_r. Induct on k to prove G^(k) is in the kernel of every irreducible of degree at most d_k. For k=1, degree-one characters kill G′. For degree d_k, write χ=Ind_H^G λ with λ linear, so [G:H]=d_k. The permutation character π=Ind_H^G 1_H has degree d_k and contains 1_G once by Frobenius reciprocity; every other constituent has degree <d_k. By induction G^(k−1) kills each such constituent and hence π. The local induced-kernel lemma puts G^(k−1)≤H. Therefore G^(k)≤H′≤ker λ. Since G^(k) is normal, it lies in every conjugate of ker λ, so the exact induced-kernel formula gives G^(k)≤ker χ. For characters of smaller degree the induction hypothesis already gives the claim. At k=r every irreducible is killed; the published intersection-of-kernels theorem gives G^(r)=1.

items.title: Implications and limits for M-groups
items.statement: For finite groups, supersolvable ⇒ M-group ⇒ solvable.

references.title: Tammo tom Dieck, Representation Theory, §§4.2–4.3 and 4.6, pp. 55–59, 64–65
Wen-Wei Li, Yanqi Lake Lectures on Algebra I, §§12.5, 14.3, pp. 146–148, 162–164
SLMath, Character Theory of Finite Groups, Ch. 9, slides 374–404

items.strategy: State only the two implications proved by the earlier local theorem and Taketa corollary. In Remarks, preview the later binary tetrahedral counterexample, whose own verification establishes strictness; do not use it as a premise of this item's Statement. Distinguish Brauer’s virtual monomial induction from the M-group property.

title: Monomial Characters and M Groups — Examples

items.title: All finite dihedral groups are M-groups
items.statement: For every n≥1, D_{2n}=C_n⋊C2 is an M-group: its irreducibles are linear extensions of inversion-fixed cyclic characters or degree-two inductions from the cyclic subgroup. These give explicit inducing subgroups, without asserting uniqueness of the inducing subgroup.

references.title: Tammo tom Dieck, Representation Theory, §§4.2–4.3 and 4.6, pp. 55–59, 64–65

items.strategy: Let θ_k(r)=exp(2πik/n). Conjugation by reflection exchanges k and −k. If 2k=0 mod n, θ_k extends in two ways across the reflection because its value there can be ±1; these are linear G-characters. Otherwise inertia is C_n and the Clifford induction theorem makes Ind_{C_n}^G θ_k an irreducible of degree two; k and −k give the same one. Clifford exhausts all irreducibles. Every listed character is induced from a linear character, including the linear ones via H=G. The n=1,2 degenerate abelian cases are included.

items.title: The order-p-cubed unitriangular group is an M-group
items.statement: For every prime p, U=UT_3(F_p) has p² linear irreducibles and p−1 irreducibles of degree p, each of the latter induced from a linear character of an abelian subgroup of index p. Hence U is an M-group.

references.title: Paul Garrett, Heisenberg groups over finite fields, §§1–2, pp. 1–3
Tammo tom Dieck, Representation Theory, §§4.2–4.3 and 4.6, pp. 55–59, 64–65

items.strategy: Write elements as (x,y,z) with product (x,y,z)(x′,y′,z′)=(x+x′,y+y′,z+z′+xy′). The center and commutator subgroup are Z={(0,0,z)}; U/Z≅F_p² gives p² linears. Put H={(0,y,z)}, an abelian normal subgroup of index p. Its characters are λ_{a,b}(0,y,z)=ζ_p^{ay+bz}. Conjugation by (t,0,0) changes a by a nonzero multiple of tb while keeping b. For b≠0 the inertia of λ_{a,b} is H; Clifford gives irreducible Ind_H^U λ_{a,b} of degree p, with one orbit per b∈F_p×. The p² linears and p−1 degree-p irreducibles have squared degrees p²+(p−1)p²=p³, so they exhaust Irr(U). This direct calculation also covers p=2; Garrett’s printed proof assumes odd q.

items.title: A solvable group that is not an M-group
items.statement: The binary tetrahedral group T=Q8⋊C3 of order 24 is solvable but is not an M-group: it has a faithful irreducible complex representation of degree two, while it has no index-two subgroup.

references.title: Tammo tom Dieck, Representation Theory, §§4.2–4.3 and 4.6, pp. 55–59, 64–65

items.strategy: In the unit quaternions set u=(−1+i+j+k)/2. Direct quaternion multiplication gives u³=1 and conjugation i↦k↦j↦i, so T=⟨Q8,u⟩≅Q8⋊C3 and is solvable. Map a+bi+cj+dk to the complex matrix [[a+bi,c+di],[−c+di,a−bi]]; multiplication on generators verifies a faithful embedding of unit quaternions in SU(2). Its restriction to Q8 is irreducible because the matrices for i and j have no common eigenline, hence the T-module is irreducible of degree two. Q8′={±1}; C3 cyclically permutes the three nonzero classes of Q8/{±1}≅F2², so [C3,Q8] maps onto the quotient and T′=Q8. Thus T_ab≅C3 and there is no index-two subgroup. A degree-two induction from a linear character would require such a subgroup, contradiction.

items.title: Trivial and one-dimensional monomial cases
items.statement: Every one-dimensional G-character λ is monomial via Ind_G^G λ=λ; in particular the trivial character is monomial. The trivial group is an M-group, and every finite abelian group is an M-group because all its complex irreducibles are one-dimensional.

references.title: Tammo tom Dieck, Representation Theory, §§4.2–4.3 and 4.6, pp. 55–59, 64–65
Wen-Wei Li, Yanqi Lake Lectures on Algebra I, §§12.5, 14.3, pp. 146–148, 162–164

items.strategy: Induction from G to itself is the identity. The trivial group has only its trivial irreducible. For a finite abelian group, simultaneous diagonalization or the published finite-abelian irreducible theorem makes each complex irreducible one-dimensional; apply the first observation.
